text:
Instructions for accessing the UT Dental Student Points Activity Report
This report includes data on the procedures you have completed in the clinic that count towards productivity
goals. In Epic, productivity is quantified by "RVU". RVUs are synonymous with "Points". The data includes the
Provider name, Service date, points, procedure code and name, the patient’s name and MRN number, and the
department and location that the procedure was completed.
1. To access the report, once you are logged into Epic, use the search feature at the top screen. Type in
“Analytics Catalog” into the search field. I would recommend to “pin” on your Epic menu for quick access
when you access Analytics Catalog again. Once in the Analytics Catalog (Reports tab), Search for “UT
Dental Student Activity Points – Individual Report
2. The reports you have access will be presented as a List or as a card and includes the UT Dental Student
Activity Points – Individual
3. Click on the card, and the report will run. The report will default display is the Detailed List as shown
below with Provider, MRN and Patient Name fully displaying.

Note Enhancement: Emergency Medicine (07/29)
Purpose-built for the ED, this new note structure replaces the
traditional A&P with a Medical Decision-Making (MDM) section—
summarizing presentation, exam findings, and test results while
surfacing differential diagnoses, acute problem lists, and more. The
result: clearer clinical reasoning, smoother hand-offs, and
documentation that supports appropriate complexity-based billing.
Note Enhancement: Behavioral Health (07/29)
Clinicians can now document complex psychiatric evaluations in a
single, structured flow. The Behavioral Health note captures patient-
voiced symptoms, psychosocial history, prior treatments, substance
use, and suicidal risk—resulting in clearer insights, fewer edits, and
more complete, stigma-free records.
Power Editing: Redraft (07/29)
With Redraft, clinicians can flip any note between styles like Concise
and Comprehensive or swap in specific Physical Exam templates—
all without reprocessing—letting users refresh individual sections in
seconds, keeping documentation perfectly aligned with each
encounter.
Note Enhancement Expansion: Emergency
Medicine (08/26)
All emergency medicine clinicians can now benefit from a
consistent, focused MDM structure—supporting clearer reasoning,
faster hand-offs, and complexity-based billing accuracy.
New Note Type: Surgical Specialties
Better A&P representation of surgical risks, findings, and outcomes
focused on necessity, with improved capture of surgical tolerance
and reasoning.
Note Enhancement: Orthopedics
Enhancing orthopedic documentation with a surgical A&P that
captures imaging, laterality, and procedural detail—improving
clarity and billing accuracy.
Note Enhancement: Hematology/Oncology
Generating more comprehensive treatment documentation that
reflects social context, oncologic history, and improved terminology
for chemotherapy.
Note Enhancement: Neurology
Captures a detailed neurological history—including development,
handedness, and anatomy—alongside test findings, medication
plans, and a neurology-specific exam template.

Benefits of LLMs in healthcare
LLMs offer tremendous potential in healthcare. Although they aren’t perfect—and require human review—
their benefits are already transforming the field.
To better understand how Qualified Chat works, let’s first define a few key terms.
AI: Computer systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, like learning, problem
solving, decision making, visual perception, and speech recognition
Generative AI: A type of AI that creates content, including text, images, videos, and analyses
LLMs: A type of generative AI trained on large datasets that generates human-like text responses to
prompts by learning to predict which word comes next in a sequence
AI basics
Qualified Chat vs other AI tools
Qualified Chat is designed to meet healthcare professionals’ unique needs.
Security: Allows you to use generative AI in your daily work, while staying HIPAA compliant and
secure, using protected health information (PHI) and protected class filters
Multiple LLMs: Sends your prompt to the LLM that’s best suited for it
Introduction to Qualified Chat
A secure, HIPAA-compliant generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool for healthcare professionals
Get started today! The possibilities are endless.
Visit https://chat.qualifiedhealthai.com for help with a challenge in your current work.

title: Prompting 201
text:
Asks Qualified Chat to respond from the perspective of a specific type of person.
You: I am a perinatal psychiatrist caring for a pregnant patient. I plan to increase the patient’s dose of an
antidepressant. Pretend you are my patient’s obstetrician who may have concerns about the change. Write
an email outlining potential concerns and questions, so I can respond to them.
Qualified Chat: [The response would be a professional email with an organized list of questions, using technical terms
appropriate for a conversation between two clinicians.]
Alternative: Ask Qualified Chat for help anticipating patient questions related to the care plan.
Persona-based prompt
Asks Qualified Chat to show its step-by-step thought process, rather than just a final answer.
It’s useful for complex problems that require multi-step reasoning.
You: Calculate the number of RN FTEs needed for a 15-bed intensive care unit. Break the task into steps
and provide the result of each step as you perform it.
Qualified Chat: To calculate the number of RN FTEs (Full-Time Equivalents) needed for a 15-bed intensive care unit
(ICU), follow these steps:
1. Determine the nurse-to-patient ratio:
For an ICU, the typical nurse-to-patient ratio is 1:2.
Each nurse will care for 2 patients.
2. Calculate the number of nurses needed per shift:
Number of patients: 15
Nurse-to-patient ratio: 1:2
Nurses needed per shift = 15 patients / 2 patients per nurse = 7.5 nurses
Since you can't have half a nurse, round up to 8 nurses per shift.
3. Determine the number of shifts per day:
Typically, there are 3 shifts per day (8-hour shifts).

title: Qualified Chat FAQ
text:
Find answers to common questions about Qualified Chat. What it is, how it works, and how to use it effectively.
Qualified Chat FAQs
General
Information
Qualified Chat is a secure, AI-powered tool designed specifically for health systems. It provides access
to large language models (LLMs) in a controlled environment, ensuring that sensitive data stays
protected and compliant with healthcare regulations. Qualified Chat helps staff find information,
generate content, or explore ideas—safely and efficiently.
What is Qualified Chat?
An LLM is a type of AI system trained on vast amounts of data to generate human-like text responses
based on patterns it has learned, without actually understanding or thinking like humans do. Imagine if
your phone's autocomplete feature read millions of books and websites, then got really good at
guessing what should come next in any conversation.
What is an LLM?
A prompt is a specific input or instruction given to an LLM to guide its response. It can range from a
simple question to complex instructions with examples, context, or formatting requirements.
What is a prompt?
No, Qualified Chat does not use or develop its own models. It uses all state-of-the-art models from
leading AI companies, including Google (like Gemini), Anthropic (like Claude), OpenAI (like GPT-4),
Cohere (like Command), Meta (like Llama 2), and several others. This diverse model selection ensures
users have access to the best AI capabilities for their specific needs and use cases.
Does Qualified Chat use its own models?
Currently, standard chat users cannot choose which model to use when using Qualified Chat. The
platform is engineered to route a user's question to the model that is known to best answer that type of

title: Qualified Chat FAQ
text:
Currently, standard chat users cannot choose which model to use when using Qualified Chat. The
platform is engineered to route a user's question to the model that is known to best answer that type of
question in that moment. As models evolve quickly, this routing is routinely updated. If want to choose
your models or use multiple models at once, please reach out to Qualified Health directly to learn more
about LLM Explorer Assistant.
Can I choose what model Qualified Chat uses to answer my question?

title: Qualified Chat FAQ
text:
Qualified Chat FAQs
No. Qualified Chat operates in a secure, sandboxed environment where the underlying language
models do not have access to the internet. This is an intentional design decision to ensure data privacy
and security in healthcare environments. There are certain Assistants, however, that allow you to
access specific, updated knowledge bases. For example, the Clinical Trails Assistant is connected to
clinicaltrials.gov. Please reach out to Qualified Health to learn more or make suggestions about safe
web information that would generate value for your team.
Is Qualified Chat connected to the internet?
The LLMs inside Qualified Chat have been trained on a broad and massive range of data up to a
specific cutoff date. They draw on patterns and knowledge from that training to generate responses to
general questions. They can answer questions about specific information if you attach it to the chat or
work through Qualified Chat’s connections to your enterprise data via Assistants.
If the model isn’t connected to the internet, how does it answer questions?
Qualified Chat can be extremely helpful, but like all LLMs, it is not infallible. It can occasionally
"hallucinate" or confidently present incorrect information. Always verify critical facts, especially in clinical
or operational contexts.
Can I trust the answers it gives?

User data is protected through strong encryption methods, role-based access controls, regular security

Data Handling
User privacy is maintained through strict adherence to HIPAA regulations, data encryption, and access

Yes, users can request data deletion at any time. Contact our support team to initiate the data deletion

Guidance for appropriate use
14
Foundational AI models carry inherent risks - susceptible to data drift, bias, and hallucinations
Healthcare amplifies these risks - without proper grounding, inaccuracies can impact patient care
Clinical decision-making without verification is prohibited - AI cannot determine or provide care insights without
verified accuracy controls (e.g., cited sources)
Appropriate uses support daily operations:
● Text and document summarization
● Writing tone and formality adjustments
● Ideation and brainstorming
● Transcription and summarization
Caregiver accountability remains absolute - providers are responsible for all AI-generated content and outputs

Three elements of effective prompts
17
Clarity
Avoid vague questions, specialized terms, and filler words. Instead, use simple and direct language.
Maybe you could tell me how to improve patient safety.
Give me strategies for preventing patient falls in an inpatient hospital.
Context
Include background information that would influence the response, like audience, goals, etc.
I work in an inpatient cardiac step-down unit with many new-graduate nurses. Give me strategies
for preventing patient falls during shift changes.
Constraints
Define the format, length, or style of the response you want.
I work in an inpatient cardiac step-down unit with many elderly patients. Give me strategies for
preventing patient falls during shift changes. Write the recommendations in the form of an email to
new nurses. Only include evidence-based strategies published in journals, such as the Journal of
Nursing Administration or the Journal of Clinical Nursing.

comprehensive response.
24
You: “You are a highly skilled meeting planner helping me create a meeting agenda. Ask me questions, one
at a time, to create a productive meeting for my team.”
Qualified Chat: “What are the main objectives or goals of the meeting?

text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Next-level prompting techniques
Few-shot prompt: Ask Qualified Chat to provide a response, based on examples
of the task and the desired output.
25
You: Generate a polite email response to a patient complaint.
Example 1 input: “Today I had to wait for over an hour for my doctor’s appointment.”
Example 1 output: Dear [patient name], I’m very sorry to hear that you had a long wait to see your physician today. At times there can be delays
because our physicians are attending to urgent matters or need more time to give a patient the care they need. We know that your time is
valuable, and we sincerely apologize for the inconvenience.
Example 2 input: “I don’t understand why I’m being charged so much for my last appointment.”
Example 2 output: Hello [patient name], Thank you for reaching out to us. We understand that bills can be confusing to interpret. Our billing
department would be happy to walk you through your statement. Please call us at your convenience at [phone number]. We are here to help you
between 9am-5pm Monday through Friday.
New input: “Your parking garage fees are too high. I shouldn’t have to pay so much to visit the doctor.”
Generate output:
Qualified Chat: [The response would be a polite email, acknowledging the concern while noting that the health system
regularly reviews its parking policies to ensure they are fair and reasonable for patients.]

title: Qualified Chat Training Webinar Slides
id: file:Shared Documents/Qualified Chat Training Webinar Slides.pdf#25
text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Next-level prompting techniques
Chain-of-thought prompt: Ask Qualified Chat to show its step-by-step thought
process, rather than just a final answer.
26
You: Calculate the number of RN FTEs needed for a 15-bed intensive care unit. Break the task into steps
and provide the result of each step as you perform it.
Qualified Chat: To calculate the number of RN FTEs (Full-Time Equivalents) needed for a 15-bed intensive care unit
(ICU), follow these steps:
1. Determine the nurse-to-patient ratio: For an ICU, the typical nurse-to-patient ratio is 1:2. Each nurse will care for 2 patients.
2. Calculate the number of nurses needed per shift: (Number of patients: 15) (Nurse-to-patient ratio: 1:2) (Nurses needed per shift = 15
patients/2 patients per nurse = 7.5 nurses) Since you can't have half a nurse, round up to 8 nurses per shift.
3. Determine the number of shifts per day: Typically, there are 3 shifts per day (8-hour shifts).
The full response would then calculate the total number of nurse shifts needed per day, the total number of
nurse shifts needed per week, and the number of hours worked by one FTE per week. And with that
information, it would calculate the total number of FTEs needed.

Pending Orders
Clinical support staff can pend orders and send them via In Basket using the Pend & Send button on the Visit

• For most encounter types, this appears as a message in the Pending Orders folder
• Orders from telephone-type encounters that contain medications are sent as Rx Request messages

Manage Pending Orders Efficinetly *Providers Only*
The Pending Orders folder in In Basket now lets you view and act on both medication and non-medication
orders without leaving In Basket. An automated response is sent to both the nurse pool and the patient based
on the decision of the request.
When a patient has multiple pended orders all the orders will appear in your Sign/Edit Orders screen for you
to Sign and Route together.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx
title: Summarize Notes with Generative AI
id: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx#0
text:
Summarize Notes is a new activity we designed to summarize a subset of a patient's notes to save you time getting up to speed about recent medical developments for a patient you haven’t seen recently or have never seen before. The system identifies recent notes of interest, or you can select specific notes of interest, and the system uses AI to generate a short summary of pertinent details. You can click links to references in the summary to see the full notes when you need more context.
We are gathering feedback from a small group of users at a variety of organizations to improve the tools using this new framework before they are broadly available. In particular, we are hoping to learn more about the following:
- What types of notes you usually select in certain contexts
- How much time you generally spend reading summaries
- How did access to summaries change the amount of time you spend on review?
- What feedback do you have about summary quality?
- Whether the summary ever included information that was incorrect
You can help us make our tools more useful and valuable for clinicians and patients everywhere by trying out the activity and submitting your feedback and suggestions.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx
title: Summarize Notes with Generative AI
id: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx#1
text:
Chart summaries are generated automatically for patients with qualifying upcoming appointments 36 hours before a scheduled encounter so that they're ready for you to read ahead of seeing the patient. To ensure you have up-to-date information, when the system detects that there have been changes to the patient's record since the summary was created, it automatically starts creating a new summary.
The instructions below describe how you can generate summaries ad hoc for patients who don't have upcoming encounters or modify summaries that were generated overnight, but you only need to complete these steps if the summary you see doesn't fit your needs.
There are two ways to generate a summary. You can either let the system choose relevant notes or manually select the notes you want summarized.
Automatically Select Notes
In this workflow, the system selects as many recent notes as possible until it either reaches the content limit for summarization or reaches 30 notes. The system automatically excludes notes that are very long, marked sensitive, or incomplete. We recommended this option because it saves you clicks selecting notes and prevents you from selecting a note that can't be summarized.
- The Summarize Notes sidebar opens automatically.
- Optionally, enter a free-text focus in the Focus On field if you want the summary to focus on a particular topic. For example, enter "blood pressure" to include information about blood pressure. You can also deselect notes you don't want included in the summary in the Notes that can be summarized section.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx
title: Summarize Notes with Generative AI
id: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx#2
text:
- Click Generate Summary. Your summary appears in the Auto-Generated Summary section. Keep in mind, it's typical for summary generation to take some time. Most summaries take 8 to 10 seconds, but some could take several minutes. You'll see a loading animation, and you can continue working in other parts of the chart while you wait. You can also click Cancel to end in-progress summary generation.
- Read your summary. If you want to read a note that contributed to the summary, click the reference link to open that note or hover over the link to see when the encounter took place, whom the patient saw, and the specialty. In the References section, you can also see a list of the summarized notes, including when the encounter took place and whom the patient saw.
- As needed, you can create a new summary. You can either:
- Generate a new summary with a new focus in the Focus field. After you click Generate Summary again, the new summary appears above up to three previous summaries from the session so you can easily compare them. If you included a focus, it appears in the summary header to help you differentiate versions of the summary. Previous summaries are available for up to 48 hours after you create them.
- Generate a new summary from a new set of notes. Refer to the Manually Select Notes section below.
Manually Select Notes
In this workflow, you select the specific notes that you want to be included in your summary.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx
title: Summarize Notes with Generative AI
id: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx#3
text:
- Generate a new summary from a new set of notes. Refer to the Manually Select Notes section below.
Manually Select Notes
In this workflow, you select the specific notes that you want to be included in your summary.
Some notes you select in this workflow might not be possible to summarize. Specifically, notes that are too long, notes that are not complete, and notes that have been marked sensitive are excluded from summarization. This filtering ensures that a summary can be generated and prevents either incomplete information from giving an incorrect impression of the patient's state or sensitive information from being exposed. These notes appear in the Notes that can't be summarized section along with the reason they can't be included.
- From a patient chart, open Chart Review (search: Chart Review) and select the Notes tab. The Summarize Notes sidebar opens.
- Hold CTRL and click to select notes you want to include in your summary. You can also hold SHIFT and click to select adjacent notes. You can select up to 30 notes.
- Click Summarize Selected, either in the activity toolbar or from the right-click menu.
- Optionally, enter a free-text focus in the Focus On field if you want the summary to focus on a particular topic. For example, enter "blood pressure" to include information about blood pressure.
- Click Generate Summary. Your summary appears in the Auto-Generated Summary section. Keep the following in mind:

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx
title: Summarize Notes with Generative AI
id: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx#4
text:
- Click Generate Summary. Your summary appears in the Auto-Generated Summary section. Keep the following in mind:
- It is typical for summary generation to take some time. Most summaries take 8 to 10 seconds, but some could take several minutes. You'll see a loading animation, and you can continue working in other parts of the chart while you wait. You can also click Cancel to end in-progress summary generation.
- You might see warnings indicating that the notes you have selected exceed the maximum character count the activity can summarize. Using the percentages as a guide, unselect notes in the Notes that can be summarized section until the character count is below the maximum allowed, 100%.
- You might see a warning indicating that not all notes could be summarized. This can occur for several reasons, including when notes are marked sensitive, when a note documented at another organization fails to download, and when you've a note that is too long or too short to summarize
- Read your summary. If you want to read a note that contributed to the summary, click the reference link to open it or hover over the link to see when the encounter took place, whom the patient saw, and the specialty. In the References section, you can also see a list of the summarized notes, including when the encounter took place and whom the patient saw.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx
title: Summarize Notes with Generative AI
id: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx#5
text:
- All the notes you have selected are analyzed, but the system might determine that some of them contain no information related to either your specialty or to the focus you entered. Information from these notes isn’t included in the summary, but these notes are listed in the References section.
- As needed, you can create a new summary. You can either:
- Generate a new summary from the same set of notes you selected in step 2. You can change which notes you have selected in the Notes that can be summarized section of the sidebar or enter a different focus, then click Summarize Selected again to see a summary based on the new input. After you click Generate Summary again, the new summary appears above up to three previous summaries from the session so you can easily compare them. If you included a focus, it appears in the summary header to help you differentiate versions of the summary. Previous summaries are available for up to 48 hours after you create them.
- Generate a new summary from a new set of notes. In Chart Review, select a set of notes as you did in step 2 and click Summarize Selected. After you click Generate Summary again, previously created summaries are cleared.
Be creative and experiment with the notes you include. In this early phase of development, we encourage you to push the limitations of the model so we can learn about its strengths and weaknesses and make it a more useful tool.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx
title: Summarize Notes with Generative AI
id: file:Shared Documents/Summarize Notes with Generative AI.docx#6
text:
When you have criticism or insights you want to share, you can do so from the activity itself.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#0
text:
WEBVTT
1
00:00:05.664 --> 00:00:18.094
Steven Mortimer: Thank you all for joining. My name is Steven Mortimer, I'm an engagement manager with Qualified Health. I'm a dedicated resource for UTSA to make sure that the deployment of Qualified Health, the platform.
2
00:00:18.094 --> 00:00:27.084
Steven Mortimer: is successful, and I can support you all in what your needs are as far as chat, but also building customized assistance and workflows in the tool itself.
3
00:00:27.254 --> 00:00:40.804
Steven Mortimer: Other folks on my team, they're not here today, are Heaton Patel, he's our Head of Customer Operations, and Rose Maher, as well as an engagement manager. The executive leadership of our team have decades of experience in healthcare, but also in technology.
4
00:00:40.884 --> 00:00:48.714
Steven Mortimer: They're actively involved in working with, Dr. Sankari, who is our executive sponsor, and others, to make sure that this is a success.
5
00:00:50.794 --> 00:00:55.353
Steven Mortimer: You're here today, and want to thank you first for making time late,
6
00:00:55.354 --> 00:01:12.813
Steven Mortimer: on a weekday here to listen to more about qualified health, but what we'd ask of you is to be an early adopter of the platform, log in, start using it for whatever application you think would be good, and then share success stories with your colleagues, and try to model best practices for them so that they can get the most out of the platform as well.
7
00:01:14.324 --> 00:01:25.113

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#1
text:
7
00:01:14.324 --> 00:01:25.113
Steven Mortimer: Before we dive in, I do think it's helpful because folks may be coming from other backgrounds or levels of experience or exposure to AI that we just defined some terms.
8
00:01:25.114 --> 00:01:39.883
Steven Mortimer: So, AI, artificial intelligence, we define as a computer that is performing a task that typically requires human intelligence. Generative AI is a subset of that, which is the creation of content, and that could be text, images, or video.
9
00:01:40.134 --> 00:01:50.454
Steven Mortimer: I mention this because Qualified Health, our platform, specifically focuses on the applications of generative AI in healthcare, and particularly ones revolving around text.
10
00:01:51.374 --> 00:02:07.583
Steven Mortimer: The abbreviation LLM, Large Language Model, is just the mode, or the vehicle, the algorithm that allows us to be able to generate this content to be generative AI. And that's models trained on a vast library of information, typically from the web.
11
00:02:09.844 --> 00:02:29.264
Steven Mortimer: So Qualified Health, what we do is we have infrastructure to be able to deploy generative AI, but also evaluate it and govern it. We have 3 products within the platform. One that we'll talk about today is Qualified Chat, so that's your chat experience, just like ChatGPT or Claude or other that you may have experienced.
12
00:02:29.314 --> 00:02:53.313

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#2
text:
12
00:02:29.314 --> 00:02:53.313
Steven Mortimer: But ours is a little bit different in that it's a HIPAA-compliant, FERPA-compliant instance of it that runs in a dedicated virtual private cloud specifically for UT San Antonio. So anything that you put into that chat is isolated to a very specific cloud that's retained and contained only for UT San Antonio. What's transmitted to our vendors, the model vendors, so OpenAI and Anthropic.
13
00:02:53.504 --> 00:03:03.704
Steven Mortimer: We have a BAA with them that none of the data can be retained for training purposes, and it's, never, copied anywhere else, so…
14
00:03:03.904 --> 00:03:16.144
Steven Mortimer: Rest assured that whatever information you put in, and you can put in patient info… protected patient information and student information, it'll only live within this dedicated virtual private client that we have your platform running in.
15
00:03:16.764 --> 00:03:36.414
Steven Mortimer: For the assistance, essentially, you can think of that product that we have in the platform as customized versions of qualified chat. So for Qualified Chat, when you work with it, every time you want to, have a conversation, you have to prompt it and provide all the context and the documents required to work through whatever task you're trying to perform.
16
00:03:36.474 --> 00:03:50.273
Steven Mortimer: An assistant, essentially, is a prepackaged set of instructions that you can define as a user, and knowledge documents that you can reference, so that you don't have to, for every conversation, provide a specific prompt.
17
00:03:50.464 --> 00:04:02.614

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#3
text:
17
00:03:50.464 --> 00:04:02.614
Steven Mortimer: or a specific set of documents that need to be uploaded. You can actually define that as the assistant, and then just chat with that directly. And you can also share assistance with colleagues so that they can also leverage them as well.
18
00:04:02.864 --> 00:04:11.134
Steven Mortimer: End-to-end workflows is the last product. Essentially, what we do is we find business processes that could be made better or more efficient with AI.
19
00:04:11.404 --> 00:04:18.904
Steven Mortimer: We work with a specific team to document their workflow and business process, apply the AI to it.
20
00:04:18.904 --> 00:04:36.133
Steven Mortimer: and then have them view results in the platform itself to be able to accomplish a task. An example of this is bed status or utilization review. Patients who get admitted to MSRH, they could be under an inpatient admission or an observational stay.
21
00:04:36.194 --> 00:04:56.834
Steven Mortimer: And so we have AI that looks at the clinical documentation of the encounter in real time and tries to determine and assess whether that patient should be in inpatient admission or not. The implication is quite large from a billing and revenue standpoint, and so that's a really interesting use case. Workflows are generally geared towards tangible ROI associated with business processes.
22
00:04:57.054 --> 00:05:03.794
Steven Mortimer: And as part of what we do, is we do trainings like this, and we work with individual departments and teams and people
23
00:05:03.794 --> 00:05:17.414

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#4
text:
22
00:04:57.054 --> 00:05:03.794
Steven Mortimer: And as part of what we do, is we do trainings like this, and we work with individual departments and teams and people
23
00:05:03.794 --> 00:05:17.414
Steven Mortimer: to help them think about the adoption of AI across the enterprise, so across UTSA. I'm sure you have lots of other AI tools. We're here to support you and the journey that you all are on as far as adopting AI.
24
00:05:19.404 --> 00:05:43.254
Steven Mortimer: What's unique about our platform, and what I really want to emphasize, is the safety and effectiveness components of it. So, we're not just any old vendor that's giving you access to LLMs. We have a specific operating system in place that is checking… well, prompts are submitted for errors, for PHI and PAI exposure.
25
00:05:43.284 --> 00:05:53.754
Steven Mortimer: And mitigating things like toxicity, bias, and hallucinations. So we're monitoring that in real time so that we understand the system that you're interacting with is performing to a level that we would expect.
26
00:05:54.544 --> 00:06:13.563
Steven Mortimer: There's also an administrative dashboard so that folks can see how the platform is being used, and in a very general sense, so that they know people are generally trying to perform this particular type of task in chat, they're interacting with these assistants that have been created that perform a particular task.
27
00:06:13.814 --> 00:06:20.343
Steven Mortimer: They are working through a particular workflow and reviewing X number of cases. This allows us to understand
28
00:06:20.844 --> 00:06:32.173

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#5
text:
27
00:06:13.814 --> 00:06:20.343
Steven Mortimer: They are working through a particular workflow and reviewing X number of cases. This allows us to understand
28
00:06:20.844 --> 00:06:32.173
Steven Mortimer: what's working well, and what may be underutilized, and helping refine that sort of adoption over time as an organization. Also embedded in the platform are governance controls, so that
29
00:06:32.364 --> 00:06:52.553
Steven Mortimer: administrators can toggle on and off access to certain features. And so I'll highlight in our tool where there's certain features that you may or may not have access to, depending on your role and what types of projects you're involved in. But all these things are part of the platform itself, so that we have a really good understanding of how it's operating.
30
00:06:53.194 --> 00:07:13.864
Steven Mortimer: And the slide here is just reiterating what I had mentioned before, is that guiding principles for our company is to make sure that AI is leveraged safely and effectively in healthcare. We're a public benefit corporation, so we have a specific mandate to talk about how we're advancing that mission within healthcare more broadly.
31
00:07:13.884 --> 00:07:24.314
Steven Mortimer: Everything we do is evaluated pre-deployment, so our release schedule is every two weeks. We're generally pushing new features, and before every time we do that, we have specific
32
00:07:24.394 --> 00:07:32.673
Steven Mortimer: Evaluations that run to check there aren't any regressions, to check there aren't changes that are not noted before in other models and things like that.
33
00:07:32.674 --> 00:07:46.563

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#6
text:
32
00:07:24.394 --> 00:07:32.673
Steven Mortimer: Evaluations that run to check there aren't any regressions, to check there aren't changes that are not noted before in other models and things like that.
33
00:07:32.674 --> 00:07:46.563
Steven Mortimer: And part of what I mentioned before with the governance piece is to ensure that they're safe and appropriate use. I'll go through some example cases of how we think you should use the chat, and other cases where you may want to rely on other sources or your clinical judgment.
34
00:07:47.394 --> 00:07:49.234
Steven Mortimer: Specifically in the clinical setting.
35
00:07:50.014 --> 00:07:53.404
Steven Mortimer: And before we dive into that, generally, we think
36
00:07:53.814 --> 00:08:04.354
Steven Mortimer: it's helpful to approach your use with AI with a framework. And so there's a particular framework that we like called the AI Fluency Framework, developed by two professors,
37
00:08:04.354 --> 00:08:14.423
Steven Mortimer: Dockin and Feller, and I'll go through that now quickly. Essentially, they talk about AI and its use, really, with three modalities, automation, augmentation, and agency.
38
00:08:14.424 --> 00:08:24.924
Steven Mortimer: And, these are not necessarily mutually exclusive. You may go through, in a period of your interaction with Qualified Chat, these different modalities, but it's helpful to think about how you're
39
00:08:24.924 --> 00:08:34.984
Steven Mortimer: expecting and interacting with the chat so that you could tailor your workflow appropriately. So automation, that's, examples where.
40
00:08:34.984 --> 00:08:48.034

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt
title: [Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Transcript] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.txt#7
text:
39
00:08:24.924 --> 00:08:34.984
Steven Mortimer: expecting and interacting with the chat so that you could tailor your workflow appropriately. So automation, that's, examples where.
40
00:08:34.984 --> 00:08:48.034
Steven Mortimer: you're summarizing a meeting, you're drafting a message, you're saying, just do this particular task for me. Augmentation is you could be asking it to brainstorm or co-write for you. And so that's an example where you may say, write a draft for me, now change some

00:09:29.544 --> 00:09:32.034

00:09:32.414 --> 00:09:42.923

00:11:28.854 --> 00:11:35.224

00:11:38.114 --> 00:11:51.163

00:11:51.274 --> 00:12:05.834

Steven Mortimer: What I mentioned before is that you can save prompts. So, at the bottom of the response, you can click this button, which is a bookmark, to essentially take the prompt that I had entered to generate this response, and then push it over here into your saved library.
142

text:
142
00:25:50.374 --> 00:26:05.223
Steven Mortimer: You also have the option, and we'd encourage you for your feedback, to give us feedback. Tell us if it's a good response or a bad response. And then you can also, because we're using different models within the platform, check which model was used.
143
00:26:05.224 --> 00:26:18.253
Steven Mortimer: If you don't select a model, so for example, I have auto-selection on, what it'll do is it'll, based on your prompt, choose the one that it believes would be best suited to handle that particular task.
144
00:26:19.834 --> 00:26:41.984
Steven Mortimer: Once you start having… start a conversation, everything within that conversation is retained in the context, so you can write another prompt, and it'll already be aware of what you've already written and uploaded and things like that. What you'll notice in the top right is that the uploaded files are noted here.
145
00:26:42.844 --> 00:27:03.983
Steven Mortimer: What also, while I'm up here in the top right, is that you can share a conversation. You would just type someone's email address. What's important to note is that when you share a conversation, the person who receives it won't be able to interact with the conversation. It'll just be a read-only copy. Also, if you were to share it, and then come back to the conversation and add more, they won't be able to see those updates.
146
00:27:06.034 --> 00:27:16.523
Steven Mortimer: Also, on this top bar here, so this title is automatically generated based on the type of information that it's coming up with.
147
00:27:16.784 --> 00:27:22.274

text:

00:27:06.034 --> 00:27:16.523

00:27:16.784 --> 00:27:22.274

00:27:23.134 --> 00:27:30.644

00:27:31.684 --> 00:27:40.183
Steven Mortimer: But, as I was mentioning before, all the context is saved here, so if I wanted to provide another prompt, and I want to…
150
00:27:40.814 --> 00:27:53.373
Steven Mortimer: take this and rewrite it for a particular grade level. I just have to say, rewrite this. I don't have to start over and upload the document and say, create a patient-facing version of this. I can just say, rewrite this.
151
00:27:53.374 --> 00:28:06.583
Steven Mortimer: what I've previously gotten, and make it at an 8th grade reading level. And the example here is that you may have, or coming into a clinical setting, a really long history, you may not be familiar with it.
152
00:28:06.584 --> 00:28:18.903
Steven Mortimer: You want to update the family, or another colleague, potentially, so you want the summary, and you may want a simpler version, or a version that's a little bit easier to understand for someone who doesn't have a medical background.
153
00:28:18.904 --> 00:28:21.973
Steven Mortimer: then you can… Prompt to get that response.
154
00:28:22.234 --> 00:28:28.944

text:

00:28:18.904 --> 00:28:21.973
Steven Mortimer: then you can… Prompt to get that response.

00:28:29.394 --> 00:28:38.213

If I were to start to describe something else in here, it'll kind of start to get confused between what I was asking it before and what I may be asking if it's related to a different topic. So if you're going to do something completely different, it's best just to start a new chat.
158
00:29:03.574 --> 00:29:18.644
Steven Mortimer: And, that chat that I was just in, it, again, shows up on the left in chronological order, so I can always go back to the chat that I was just in if I need to. So, it's… everything's retained, you go back to new chat, you can start something fresh.
159
00:29:19.734 --> 00:29:30.143

00:29:30.144 --> 00:29:40.733

00:29:19.734 --> 00:29:30.143
Steven Mortimer: So, here I'm using a safe prompt. This is a prompt where you are a nurse manager, that's your role, and this is… this prompt in particular covers some of the

00:29:30.144 --> 00:29:40.733
Steven Mortimer: best practices that I outlined earlier in the presentation, as far as providing some context in your role. So you're a nurse manager, you're in a large health system, you're planning for a quarterly leadership meeting.
161
00:29:40.974 --> 00:29:59.443
Steven Mortimer: you've identified an increase in infections, and particularly catheter-associated urinary tract infections on L&D. And so you could ask it to come up with a quality improvement plan for you. And what Qualified Chat and what many LLMs are good at doing is coming up with a really structured, comprehensive first draft.
162
00:29:59.594 --> 00:30:02.123
Steven Mortimer: So, for a quality improvement plan.
163
00:30:02.634 --> 00:30:07.733
Steven Mortimer: of this nature, it should spit out in a second here,
164
00:30:08.484 --> 00:30:27.884
Steven Mortimer: a really nice summary that starts with, well, what is the background and aim of this particular program? So, the current state and what we aim to do, and it fills it in with information already. You would have to go back and edit this as you see fit, but it's really good at coming up with this structure.
165
00:30:28.114 --> 00:30:38.033
Steven Mortimer: And if you wanted to, again, follow up with a different spin on this, which is, okay, we've got this quality improvement program, how would we start a training

00:30:38.034 --> 00:30:49.774

text:
165
00:30:28.114 --> 00:30:38.033

00:30:38.034 --> 00:30:49.774

167
00:30:52.394 --> 00:31:06.563
Steven Mortimer: I'll show one last example here, and then we can open it up for questions, and that's, Qualified Chat, is also good at summarizing documents. So, for example, there's a… I have a transcript from CMS webinars.

00:31:06.564 --> 00:31:14.164

170
00:31:31.424 --> 00:31:45.333
Steven Mortimer: and that you could then ask qualified chat to summarize. So if you… another good example that's very similar is if you have another platform that you use for transcribing meetings, and you want to get a summary out, or you want to interact with that, say, write action items, you could do that as well.
171
00:31:49.394 --> 00:31:53.383
Steven Mortimer: So I think that's, plenty of examples. I wanna…
172

00:33:09.604 --> 00:33:13.303
Jose Cavazos: I apologize, but I missed the first 5 minutes.

00:33:13.304 --> 00:33:27.744

00:33:29.124 --> 00:33:37.814

00:33:27.964 --> 00:33:28.784
Steven Mortimer: Environment?

00:33:29.124 --> 00:33:37.814
Jose Cavazos: So it's not training, even though that you may be selecting Claude, or Gemini, or… it doesn't train their engines.
186
00:33:38.054 --> 00:34:00.243
Steven Mortimer: Yeah, so we put it in the virtual private cloud so that you in the application can reference prior conversations, you can share conversations, all of that. Whenever you have to interact with any of the external models, we have a business agreement that it's zero retention, and none of it would be used for training. So, essentially, it exists for the time on their servers to be able to generate the response, and then it's deleted.
187
00:34:00.244 --> 00:34:01.903
Steven Mortimer: And then it comes back to us.
188
00:34:02.363 --> 00:34:21.213
Steven Mortimer: So none of that is used to train models, and actually, we don't train any models ourselves, so for some of the workflows that I mentioned earlier, we'll use the LLM, and we'll prompt it, and we'll tune what we would use to get different outputs, but we actually ourselves are not, like, a vendor which will take
189
00:34:21.214 --> 00:34:34.553
Steven Mortimer: years of your prior data and train on it to build anything ourselves. We do this specific to your institution and use out-of-the-box algorithms and LLMs to then apply to your situation.

00:34:35.084 --> 00:34:38.193

00:36:56.174 --> 00:37:07.994

00:37:08.104 --> 00:37:23.774
Steven Mortimer: So, I mean, there's definitely ways in which we can… you can interact and you can call this yourself with individual patient records, but if you were to get to a point where you're talking about hundreds of records, it's just not feasible to interact with this UI, we could call it programmatically to be able to identify certain things.

00:37:56.804 --> 00:38:09.363

00:38:09.594 --> 00:38:12.324
Steven Mortimer: pre-built…

00:38:12.604 --> 00:38:24.403

00:38:24.994 --> 00:38:39.164
Steven Mortimer: Not exactly the scenario you're describing, but similar in which we have already instructions, and some basic guidelines on how to take a particular type of input, and then repeat it back in a particular format that would be more useful.

00:38:39.384 --> 00:38:59.364

AI Fluency Framework
Developed by professors Rick Dakan and Joseph Feller, the framework highlights the human skills that unlock AI’s potential in
meaningful, responsible ways.
11
Dakan, Rick and Feller, Joseph. "Framework for AI Fluency (Practical Summary Document)," Version 1.1, Ringling.edu/ai/, 2025. https://ringling.libguides.com/ai/framework Retrieved on June 11, 2025. License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
AI Fluency:
The ability to confidently understand, evaluate, and collaborate with AI tools to
solve problems, enhance decision-making, and spark innovation—while
recognizing the risks, limitations, and ethical considerations that come with it.

text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Ways people engage with AI
12
The AI Fluency Framework outlines three key modalities:
When AI carries out clear,
specific tasks that you
request—like summarizing a
meeting or drafting a message
Automation Augmentation
When you work together, with AI
serving as your tireless thought
partner—brainstorming,
co-writing, or co-analyzing
Agency
When you design the AI to act
more independently—like
chatbots, tutors, or digital agents
running in the background
Dakan, Rick and Feller, Joseph. "Framework for AI Fluency (Practical Summary Document)," Version 1.1, Ringling.edu/ai/, 2025. https://ringling.libguides.com/ai/framework Retrieved on June 11, 2025. License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Four core competencies for effective AI collaboration
13
Dakan, Rick and Feller, Joseph. "Framework for AI Fluency (Practical Summary Document)," Version 1.1, Ringling.edu/ai/, 2025. https://ringling.libguides.com/ai/framework Retrieved on June 11, 2025. License: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
Ask: What’s the goal? What needs human insight or
empathy? What could AI help accelerate or simplify?
1. Delegation
Decide what AI should handle and what
you should do yourself.
Product: What do you want it to create?
Process: How should it approach the task?
Performance: What tone or style should it use?
2. Description
Give clear, structured instructions, also
known as prompting.
Ask: Is this actually what I needed? Does the
reasoning hold up? Is the tone right for my audience?
3. Discernment
Determine whether AI gives you a good
response.
Ask: Have I verified the information? Have I been
transparent about AI’s role in the process? Are there
any risks, like potential bias?
4. Diligence
Assess if you are using AI responsibly
and with integrity.

text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Qualified Chat overview
Qualified Chat provides health system staff with access to large language models (LLMs) in a controlled
environment, ensuring that sensitive data stays protected and compliant with healthcare regulations.
Find information, generate content, and explore ideas—safely and efficiently.
15
Platform leverages
multiple LLMs
Qualified Chat uses state-of-the-art models from leading AI companies:
Google (like Gemini), Anthropic (like Claude), OpenAI (like GPT-4),
Cohere (like Command), Meta (like Llama 4), and several others.
It’s engineered to route to the model that best answers each question. As models evolve quickly, this routing is routinely updated.

text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Guidance for appropriate use
16
Foundational AI models carry inherent risks - susceptible to data drift, bias, and hallucinations
Healthcare amplifies these risks - without proper grounding, inaccuracies can impact patient care
Clinical decision-making without verification is prohibited - AI cannot determine or provide care insights without
verified accuracy controls (e.g., cited sources)
Appropriate uses support daily operations:
● Text and document summarization
● Writing tone and formality adjustments
● Ideation and brainstorming
● Transcription and summarization
Caregiver accountability remains absolute - providers are responsible for all AI-generated content and outputs

text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Three elements of effective prompts
20
Clarity
Avoid vague questions, specialized terms, and filler words. Instead, use simple and direct language.
Maybe you could tell me how to improve patient safety.
Give me strategies for preventing patient falls in an inpatient hospital.
Context
Include background information that would influence the response, like audience, goals, etc.
I work in an inpatient cardiac step-down unit with many new-graduate nurses. Give me strategies
for preventing patient falls during shift changes.
Constraints
Define the format, length, or style of the response you want.
I work in an inpatient cardiac step-down unit with many elderly patients. Give me strategies for
preventing patient falls during shift changes. Write the recommendations in the form of an email to
new nurses. Only include evidence-based strategies published in journals, such as the Journal of
Nursing Administration or the Journal of Clinical Nursing.

text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Next-level prompting techniques
Persona-based prompt: Ask Qualified Chat to respond from the perspective of a
specific type of person.
26
You: I am a perinatal psychiatrist caring for a pregnant patient. I plan to increase the patient’s dose of an
antidepressant. Pretend you are my patient’s obstetrician who may have concerns about the change. Write
an email outlining potential concerns and questions, so I can respond to them.
Qualified Chat: [The response would be a professional email with an organized list of questions, using technical terms
appropriate for a conversation between two clinicians.]
Alternative: Ask Qualified Chat for help anticipating patient questions related to the care plan.

title: [Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.pdf#26
text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Next-level prompting techniques
Interview prompt: Ask Qualified Chat to gather information it needs to provide a
comprehensive response.
27
You: “You are a highly skilled meeting planner helping me create a meeting agenda. Ask me questions, one
at a time, to create a productive meeting for my team.”
Qualified Chat: “What are the main objectives or goals of the meeting?
You: “The objective of the meeting is to evaluate a proposal to increase utilization of our patient portal for scheduling
appointments.”
Qualified chat might next ask, “How long do you anticipate the meeting will last?” And after multiple rounds
of question-and-answer exchange, it would produce a well-structured agenda, tailored to your needs.

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.pdf
title: [Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.pdf#27
text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Next-level prompting techniques
Few-shot prompt: Ask Qualified Chat to provide a response, based on examples
of the task and the desired output.
28
You: Generate a polite email response to a patient complaint.
Example 1 input: “Today I had to wait for over an hour for my doctor’s appointment.”
Example 1 output: Dear [patient name], I’m very sorry to hear that you had a long wait to see your physician today. At times there can be delays
because our physicians are attending to urgent matters or need more time to give a patient the care they need. We know that your time is
valuable, and we sincerely apologize for the inconvenience.
Example 2 input: “I don’t understand why I’m being charged so much for my last appointment.”
Example 2 output: Hello [patient name], Thank you for reaching out to us. We understand that bills can be confusing to interpret. Our billing
department would be happy to walk you through your statement. Please call us at your convenience at [phone number]. We are here to help you
between 9am-5pm Monday through Friday.
New input: “Your parking garage fees are too high. I shouldn’t have to pay so much to visit the doctor.”
Generate output:
Qualified Chat: [The response would be a polite email, acknowledging the concern while noting that the health system
regularly reviews its parking policies to ensure they are fair and reasonable for patients.]

sourceId: file:Shared Documents/[Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.pdf
title: [Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025
id: file:Shared Documents/[Slides] UTSA Qualified Chat Training - November 2025.pdf#28
text:
Confidential – Not for distribution or citation – © 2024 Qualified Health
Next-level prompting techniques
Chain-of-thought prompt: Ask Qualified Chat to show its step-by-step thought
process, rather than just a final answer.
29
You: Calculate the number of RN FTEs needed for a 15-bed intensive care unit. Break the task into steps
and provide the result of each step as you perform it.
Qualified Chat: To calculate the number of RN FTEs (Full-Time Equivalents) needed for a 15-bed intensive care unit
(ICU), follow these steps:
1. Determine the nurse-to-patient ratio: For an ICU, the typical nurse-to-patient ratio is 1:2. Each nurse will care for 2 patients.
2. Calculate the number of nurses needed per shift: (Number of patients: 15) (Nurse-to-patient ratio: 1:2) (Nurses needed per shift = 15
patients/2 patients per nurse = 7.5 nurses) Since you can't have half a nurse, round up to 8 nurses per shift.
3. Determine the number of shifts per day: Typically, there are 3 shifts per day (8-hour shifts).
The full response would then calculate the total number of nurse shifts needed per day, the total number of
nurse shifts needed per week, and the number of hours worked by one FTE per week. And with that
information, it would calculate the total number of FTEs needed.

text:
Weekly:
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
Monthly:
- New users: The number of people who have never visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Returning users: The number of people who have visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
- Pages per session: Website's total page views (visits) divided by total number of sessions in a given period (aim for 1.7 to 4.0)
- Scroll depth: Measures how far a user’s scrolls on a page, 60% - 80% is a good range.
- Active time spent: How long a user is actively reading or interacting with the site (average time spent on the site), 52 seconds is average.

text:
Weekly:
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
Monthly:
- New users: The number of people who have never visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Returning users: The number of people who have visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
- Pages per session: Website's total page views (visits) divided by total number of sessions in a given period (aim for 1.7 to 4.0)
- Scroll depth: Measures how far a user’s scrolls on a page, 60% - 80% is a good range.
- Active time spent: How long a user is actively reading or interacting with the site (average time spent on the site), 52 seconds is average.

text:
Weekly:
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
Monthly:
- New users: The number of people who have never visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Returning users: The number of people who have visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
- Pages per session: Website's total page views (visits) divided by total number of sessions in a given period (aim for 1.7 to 4.0)
- Scroll depth: Measures how far a user’s scrolls on a page, 60% - 80% is a good range.
- Active time spent: How long a user is actively reading or interacting with the site (average time spent on the site), 52 seconds is average.

text:
Weekly:
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
Monthly:
- New users: The number of people who have never visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Returning users: The number of people who have visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
- Pages per session: Website's total page views (visits) divided by total number of sessions in a given period (aim for 1.7 to 4.0)
- Scroll depth: Measures how far a user’s scrolls on a page, 60% - 80% is a good range.
- Active time spent: How long a user is actively reading or interacting with the site (average time spent on the site), 52 seconds is average.

title: abridge haiku workflow for Android Users
text:
1. Open Haiku:
• Upgrade to the latest Haiku version or, if
needed, download via the Google Play Store.
2. Visit Recorder:
• Navigate to Visit Recorder for the patient in
the menu.
3. Record:
• Start the Abridge session directly within the
patient's chart in Haiku.
4. Finish:
• Tap "Create Note" - your documentation is
delivered to Epic automatically.
Abridge Haiku Workflow for Android Users
Key Features:
You no longer need to "Send to EHR" or use the Abridge for Clinicians App! By
recording inside Haiku, your note flows automatically into Epic, populating your
existing dot-phrases (.HPISEC, .APSEC, etc.) instantly.
The New Workflow

text:
Weekly:
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
Monthly:
- New users: The number of people who have never visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Returning users: The number of people who have visited your site or app before in the specified date range.
- Unique users: Distinct individuals who visit a website over a specified period, regardless of how many times they visit (counted as one unique visitor)
- Sessions: Number of visits to site based on users (returned user or new user, any user)
- Pages per session: Website's total page views (visits) divided by total number of sessions in a given period (aim for 1.7 to 4.0)
- Scroll depth: Measures how far a user’s scrolls on a page, 60% - 80% is a good range.
- Active time spent: How long a user is actively reading or interacting with the site (average time spent on the site), 52 seconds is average.

title: Abridge AI CDS
text:
Announcement flyer/email introducing Abridge AI with Clinical Decision Support (CDS), powered by UpToDate, with getting-started instructions and a webinar registration link.
**ABRIDGE**
# Abridge AI with Clinical Decision Support
**Introducing Abridge AI with CDS:** Ask any clinical question about your patient using Abridge AI and get context-aware insights from UpToDate — shaped by your conversation, cited to the source, delivered in seconds.
No extra login. No switching tools. The clinical knowledge you need, right where you're already working.
[Image: product screenshot showing three panels]
- Prompt: "What asthma step-up therapy is best for this patient?"
- Thinking...
- ✓ Request processed
- ✓ Found 7 articles
- Summarizing findings...
- Preferred regimen (per GINA and NAEPP): Low-dose ICS–formoterol used as both maintenance and reliever therapy (MART).
- UpToDate® by Wolters Kluwer — Initiating asthma therapy and monitoring in adolescents and adults.
**Try asking:**
- "What step-up therapy options are best for this patient's asthma?"
- "What workup is recommended for new-onset atrial fibrillation?"
- "Are there screening recommendations I should consider for this patient?"
Abridge will provide a response that you can include directly in your note. Just prompt to incorporate the insights.
**Built for clinical rigor.** CDS underwent extensive evaluation before reaching you — including clinical quality rubrics developed with practicing physicians, an independent clinical safety review, and beta testing with hundreds of specialists. Outputs are subject to clinician review, validation, and independent clinical judgment.
**Get Started:**
- Go to **Abridge AI** after your note is generated. Abridge Inside users can find Abridge AI within the Abridge activity tab in Hyperspace.
- **Watch the video walk-through and read the full guide by clicking here.** (hyperlink)

Thrombosed external hemorrhoid
Resolving thrombosed external hemorrhoid, initially exacerbated by weightlifting
three weeks ago. The thrombus is partially absorbed with mild residual edema and
no current pain. Surgical excision is not indicated, as intervention would not
accelerate recovery and may increase morbidity. He remains at increased risk for
recurrence, particularly with continued weightlifting.
- Recommend moist heat application, such as warm showers, to promote clot
reabsorption.
- Advise against further use of suppositories or topical creams.
- Instruct to avoid prolonged toilet sitting, constipation, and straining; encourage
adequate dietary fiber and hydration.
- Advise to contact the office within 48 hours of a new thrombosed hemorrhoid for
possible intervention.
- Provide guidance on warm soaks for symptom relief if recurrence occurs.
- Instruct to follow up if symptoms persist beyond one month or if discomfort
develops.

Chronic C5-C6 disc herniation causing neck pain, right arm numbness, and
intermittent right hand weakness. Symptoms refractory to conservative
management, causing functional impairment with risk of permanent neurological
deficit. Surgical decompression and stabilization with ACDF indicated.

- Provided education regarding diagnosis, surgical rationale, anticipated
outcomes, and risks including infection, hemorrhage, hoarseness, dysphagia,
nonunion, and rare risk of spinal cord injury or worsening symptoms.

Appropriate surgical candidate for ACDF based on symptom progression, imaging

hyperlipidemia, indicating low to moderate surgical risk.
- Initiated scheduling for ACDF.
- Arranged preoperative appointment, laboratory studies, and necessary
clearances.
- Provided educational materials regarding procedure, risks, benefits, and recovery
expectations.

Progressive C5-C6 disc herniation with spinal cord and right C6 root
compression. Conservative management failed. High risk for permanent
neurologic deficit without decompression. Explained ACDF benefits
including decompression, pain reduction, sensory improvement, prevention
of neurologic decline, and possible improvement in grip strength and
coordination. Explained risks including infection, bleeding, hoarseness,

mechanical compression and that delaying surgery increased risk of
permanent neurologic injury. Provided ACDF education and recovery
expectations of approximately 4 to 6 weeks depending on activity.

Joanne Hess is a 69 year old female with adhesive capsulitis, osteoarthritis, rotator
cuff tendinitis of the left shoulder, and residual contractures following stroke who
presents for evaluation of persistent left shoulder pain and dysfunction.
Persistent left shoulder pain and stiffness for approximately two years, with
significant limitation in range of motion. Pain radiates from the shoulder into the
fingers, which are described as tight. Marked functional impairment and persistent
frozen shoulder.
Recent left shoulder injection provided partial pain relief but did not resolve
symptoms. Aware that improvement is expected to be gradual and that the
injection was intended to facilitate therapy.
Left upper extremity dysfunction is complicated by residual contractures and
weakness following prior stroke, particularly affecting the elbow, hand, and fingers.
Tightness and contracture in the fingers, with symptoms extending from the
elbow into the hand. No history of anticoagulation or prior surgery on the affected
extremity.
Previously evaluated by another orthopedic surgeon who discussed possible
surgical intervention for the hand and elbow, but she did not proceed with surgery
and is seeking further opinions. Has participated in occupational and physical
therapy, with a preference for occupational therapy with a specific therapist.
Requests therapy referral to Pittmanshire due to prior referral issues.

text:
HOW TO TALK TO ABRIDGE
WHAT IS A PROMPT?
A prompt is simply an instruction you type to tell Abridge how to change your note.
You don't need to write code. You don't need special language. You just need to be as
clear as you'd be telling a smart colleague exactly what you want.
1. 2.
3. ASK YOURSELF THREE QUESTIONS:
Which section am I focused on? (or the whole note?)
What’s not working right now? (too long, wrong tone, missing something, wrong structure?)
What should it look like when Abridge is done fixing it?
Your prompt is just the answer to those three questions, written as a sentence.
Need help? Contact help@abridge.com4

HOW TO TALK TO ABRIDGE
YOU'RE ALWAYS IN CONTROL
Abridge's edits are a starting point, not a final draft.
Your first prompt doesn't have to be perfect. Just be honest about what you want changed.
You can:
Run another prompt if the first result isn't quite right
Be more specific the second time around—include targeted section
Ask Abridge for prompt suggestions
THERE'S NO WRONG WAY TO START
The more you use prompt editing, the faster you'll find the phrasing that works for you,
which you can save and apply the next time.

specialist, list them separately in a clearly labeled section. Include the managing specialist's
name or specialty and a brief note on the current status or plan as communicated during the
visit, without duplicating or modifying their management recommendations.

COMPREHENSIVE NOTE ENHANCEMENT (HPI + A&P)
Review the full note and identify any clinical details mentioned in the conversation that were
not captured in the initial output. For the HPI, add any missing symptom characteristics,
timeline, aggravating or relieving factors, associated symptoms, pertinent negatives, or
patient-reported history. For the assessment and plan, expand each problem to include the
clinician's reasoning for the diagnosis or differential, relevant supporting findings, treatment
rationale, specific medications or doses discussed, patient education provided, and follow-up
instructions. Do not repeat the content already present in the note. Maintain the existing
structure of both sections.9

Include all facilities involved in the patient's care transition (such as hospital, rehabilitation
facility, or skilled nursing facility), the admission date, discharge date from each facility, and

during this visit, any changes to medications or the care plan made since discharge, the

title: Qualified Chat for Patient Service Reps UTHSA Training Module
text:
QUALIFIED HEALTH × UTHSA
Qualified Chat for Patient Service Reps — UTHSA Training Module · Page 1
Qualified Chat for Patient Service Reps
Practical AI use cases for the UTHSA front-desk, scheduling, and call-center teams.
Why this matters
Patient Service Reps handle the highest message volume and most varied scripts in the clinic.
Qualified Chat is HIPAA-compliant AI that can draft replies, translate complex provider info into
patient language, generate scripts for tough calls, and handle the repetitive writing that eats
your day. Used well, it gives you 30–60 minutes back every shift.
Part 1 — How to use Qualified Chat (and when to build an Assistant)
Getting started in 60 seconds
• Log in: chat.qualifiedhealthai.com with your UTHSA email.
• Type a question or paste a message you need help with.
• Pin chats you use often — quick links beat retyping.
PHI safety (the big one)
Qualified Chat is HIPAA-compliant — it's safe to paste de-identified info. When in doubt, swap
real names/DOB/MRN for placeholders: "a patient with an appointment next Tuesday" works
just as well. NEVER paste patient identifiers into ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, or any consumer AI
— only Qualified Chat is approved at UTHSA.
Chat vs. Assistant — when to build a reusable one
Chat is a one-off conversation. An Assistant is a saved mini-app tuned to one repeated task.
Front-desk work is FULL of repeated tasks (appointment reminders, scheduling FAQs, billing
explanations) — perfect Assistant territory.
• Use Chat for: one-off rewrites, translating unusual provider notes, handling unique patient
questions.
• Use an Assistant for: appointment confirmation templates, common billing/insurance FAQs,
no-show follow-up scripts, multi-language reply drafting.
Assistants coming soon at UTHSA

Use Case 1: Draft warm appointment confirmation texts/emails
Personalize a confirmation message in 5 seconds instead of using the cold template.

insurance card, parking location."

title: Qualified Chat for Patient Service Reps UTHSA Training Module
text:
QUALIFIED HEALTH × UTHSA
Qualified Chat for Patient Service Reps — UTHSA Training Module · Page 2
Pro tip: Save the prompt — it's your first Assistant template.
Use Case 2: Translate a clinical note into something the patient understands
Patient calls confused about what the doctor said? Paste the relevant note (de-identified) and ask
Chat to explain in plain English.
"Translate this visit note into plain English for the patient. 6th-grade reading level. Skip medical
jargon. Focus on: what's wrong, what we're doing about it, what they need to do this week."
Use Case 3: Draft a de-escalation script for an upset caller
Patient is frustrated about a billing issue, long wait, or denied request? Get a calming, empathetic
script before you pick up.
"I have a frustrated patient on the line about a 45-minute wait. Give me 3 opening lines that
acknowledge their frustration without being defensive, plus a script for what I can offer
(reschedule, manager callback, see them ASAP)."
Pro tip: Roleplay back: "Now respond as the upset patient — what might they push back with?"
Use Case 4: Explain an insurance denial in plain English
Patient calls asking why their claim was denied? Paste the EOB language and ask Chat to translate.
"This is what the insurance EOB said: [paste reason]. Translate it into plain English I can read
to the patient. Explain why it was denied, what their options are (appeal, payment plan, financial
counseling), and what they should do next."
Use Case 5: Draft a follow-up message for a no-show
Patient missed their appointment? Personalize a warm follow-up instead of the auto-template.

Use Case 5: Draft a follow-up message for a no-show
Patient missed their appointment? Personalize a warm follow-up instead of the auto-template.
"Draft a follow-up message to a patient who no-showed their physical therapy appointment
yesterday. Warm tone, no guilt-tripping. Offer to reschedule and remind them PT is most
effective with consistency. Under 120 words."
Use Case 6: Translate a reply into Spanish (or any language)
Drafted a reply in English? Ask Chat to translate it.
"Translate this appointment confirmation message into Spanish. Keep the friendly tone. Use
"usted" form. Keep the same time and instructions exactly."
Pro tip: Have a native speaker spot-check before sending sensitive content the first few times.
Use Case 7: Quick "what's in the chart" summary before a call back
Patient is calling and you've got 30 seconds. Paste the recent visit summary (de-identified) and get a
3-bullet briefing.
"Summarize this patient's last visit in 3 bullets so I can speak to it intelligently when I call them
back: what they came in for, what was decided, what's pending or needs follow-up."
Use Case 8: Draft pre-visit instructions for a new patient
New patient visit coming up? Give them clear pre-visit instructions tailored to their visit type.
"Write pre-visit instructions for a new patient coming in for a colonoscopy consult. Cover: what
to bring, what to expect at the visit, no fasting required. Friendly tone, easy to skim. Under 150
words."
